Operating Systems: Virtual Memory, Paging, Page Tables, and Translation Lookaside Buffers (TLB)
Process Lifecycle, Process Control Blocks (PCB), and Context Switching mechanics
Inter-Process Communication (IPC): Anonymous Pipes, Named Pipes (FIFOs), Shared Memory, and Unix Domain Sockets
Deadlock Prevention, Detection, Coffman Conditions, and the Banker's Algorithm
File System Internals: Inodes, Directory Trees, Superblocks, and Journaling (ext4, APFS, NTFS)
CPU Scheduling Policies: Round-Robin, Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS), Multi-Level Feedback Queues
Computer Networking: Transmission Control Protocol (TCP) 3-Way Handshake (SYN, SYN-ACK, ACK) and 4-Way Connection Teardown
TCP Congestion Control Algorithms (Slow Start, Congestion Avoidance, CUBIC, BBR)
User Datagram Protocol (UDP) vs TCP: Connectionless delivery, low latency, and packet loss tolerance
Domain Name System (DNS) Recursive vs Iterative Resolution and Record Types (A, AAAA, CNAME, MX, TXT)
Transport Layer Security (TLS 1.3) Handshake, Ephemeral Diffie-Hellman Key Exchange, and AEAD Ciphers
HTTP Protocol Evolution: HTTP/1.1 Head-of-Line Blocking vs HTTP/2 Binary Multiplexing vs HTTP/3 QUIC over UDP
CIDR Subnet Masking, Variable-Length Subnet Masking (VLSM), and Autonomous System BGP Routing
Computer Architecture: CPU Cache Hierarchy: L1 Instruction/Data Caches, L2 Cache, L3 Shared Cache, and 64-byte Cache Lines
Cache Coherence Protocols: MESI (Modified, Exclusive, Shared, Invalid) and MOESI states
Instruction Pipelining and Hazards: Structural, Data (Read-After-Write), and Control (Branch Misprediction)
SIMD (Single Instruction, Multiple Data) Vector Extensions: AVX-512, ARM NEON
Memory Barriers, Sequential Consistency, and Out-of-Order Instruction Execution
RISC vs CISC Architectural Design: ARM64 / RISC-V load-store design vs x86-64 complex instruction sets
Compilers and Language Runtimes: Lexical Analysis, Tokenization, Deterministic Finite Automata (DFA), and Regular Expressions
Context-Free Grammars, LL(k) vs LR(k) / LALR Parsers, and Abstract Syntax Tree (AST) Generation
Intermediate Representation (IR), Static Single Assignment (SSA) form, and LLVM Optimization Passes
Just-In-Time (JIT) Tiered Compilation vs Ahead-Of-Time (AOT) Machine Code Generation
Garbage Collection Algorithms: Tracing (Mark-Sweep, Generational, Tri-Color Marking) vs Reference Counting with Cycle Detection
Stack vs Heap Memory Layout, Call Stack Frames, and Escape Analysis
Distributed Systems: CAP Theorem (Consistency, Availability, Partition Tolerance) and Brewer's Trade-offs
Consensus Algorithms: Raft Leader Election, Heartbeats, and Log Replication vs Multi-Paxos
Eventual Consistency Models, Conflict-Free Replicated Data Types (CRDTs), and Strong Consistency
Logical Time in Distributed Networks: Lamport Timestamps and Vector Clocks
Atomic Commit Protocols: Two-Phase Commit (2PC), Three-Phase Commit (3PC), and the Saga Pattern
Consistent Hashing with Virtual Nodes for Distributed Caching and Partitioning
Distributed Tracing, Trace Context Propagation (W3C), and OpenTelemetry Observability
Cybersecurity and IT Infrastructure: Asymmetric Public-Key Cryptography: RSA, Elliptic-Curve Cryptography (ECC), and Digital Signatures
Symmetric Encryption Standards: AES-256-GCM and ChaCha20-Poly1305 Authenticated Encryption

Identity and Access Management: OAuth 2.0 Authorization Code Flow with PKCE, OpenID Connect (OIDC), and JWT Verification

Testing Methods.Description: Alternative assessment modalities beyond multiple-choice to evaluate syntax mastery, operational order, and conceptual classification
True/False: Binary syntax validity verification (e.g., 'Is `const x := 10` valid syntax in Go? True/False')
Expression evaluation (e.g., 'In Python, does `bool([])` evaluate to True? True/False')
Language design and typing paradigm assertions (e.g., 'Rust enforces memory safety without a garbage collector. True/False')
Matching: Match language keywords and symbols to their semantics (e.g., `defer` in Go, `unsafe` in Rust, `yield` in Python)
Match algorithmic operations to their average and worst-case time complexities
Match database engines to their underlying storage engines (e.g., PostgreSQL -> heap/B-tree, Redis -> RAM/dict, Cassandra -> LSM-Tree)
Match network protocols to their OSI/TCP/IP layer (e.g., BGP -> Layer 3/4, TLS -> Layer 5/6, HTTP/3 -> Layer 7)
Sequencing: Arrange scrambled lines of code in correct syntactic and logical execution sequence (Parsons problems)
Sequence network handshake packets in correct chronological order (e.g., SYN -> SYN-ACK -> ACK)
Sequence compiler pipeline stages (Lexical Analysis -> Parsing -> Semantic Analysis -> IR Generation -> Optimization -> Code Generation)
Sequence system boot and process initialization stages (Firmware/UEFI -> Bootloader -> Kernel Init -> Init/systemd)
Sorting/Classification: Classify languages by type system: Statically Typed vs Dynamically Typed, Strongly Typed vs Weakly Typed
Classify languages by memory management: Manual Allocation (C/C++), Automatic GC (Java/Go), Borrowing/Lifetimes (Rust)
Classify databases by data model: Relational (ACID), Document, Key-Value, Wide-Column, Vector, Graph
Sort algorithmic complexities from fastest to slowest: O(1) < O(log n) < O(n) < O(n log n) < O(n^2) < O(2^n)

General Language Notes: Always declare and initialize all your variables at the beginning of your scope.
Statically typed programming languages are those in which variables need to be defined before they are used.
General DB Notes: A database system is self-describing because it not only contains the database itself, but also the meta-data which defines and describes the data and relationships between tables in the database.
Insulation between the programs and data is also called program-data independence.
A view is a subset of the database, which is defined and dedicated for particular users of the system.
Instead of using joins, NoSQL databases often use techniques such as embedding and referencing to combine data from multiple documents or collections.
The simplest form of a NoSQL database is called a Key-Value database and it's designed kind of like a dictionary.

A Document database is a type of NoSQL database that can store multiple key values in a structure called a document. Documents roughly parallel rows in a table. Keys are scalars. And values may be complex data structures such as arrays or lists.
A Wide Column database is a type of NoSQL database where the columns are not fixed and the data is denormalized. The values can be complex structures such as arrays or lists.
A Graph database is a type of NoSQL database that represents a network of connected entities. Entities are liked by edges. Entities and edges each have their own properties that can be queried.

C: C is optimal for many processing-based applications like operating systems, embedded systems, device drivers, compilers, interpreters, micro processors, and micro controllers.
C#: .NET supports structs and classes.
Structs are passed by copy, since they are value types.
Objects are passed by reference, since they are reference types
The .NET platform manages and reclaims blocks of memory
The Garbage Collector object GC is part of the system namespace.
Reference GC.GetTotalMemory(false); to see how much memory an application is using
Every object derives from the base Object class, inheriting it's methods like ToString().
C# supports the "is" operator
Protected members can be accessed by the defining class or any subclass
Private members can only be accessed by the defining class.
The "virtual" keyword indicates that the method can be overridden by subclasses.
If you don't provide a constructor for a class, the compiler will create a default one.
Testing frameworks such as NUnit make C# amenable to test-driven development and thus a good language for use with Extreme Programming.
PowerShell: Cmdlets are in the form of Verb-Noun. For example, the command Get-ChildItem can be used to list our current directory.
Dart: Type inference allows us to declare a variable without explicitly mentioning the data type.
In Dart, we can insert the var keyword in place of the data type.
If you want a variable to hold objects of many types, you can declare a variable using the dynamic keyword.
The type num is generic enough to hold both int and double.
Scala: While Scala is a pure object-oriented programming language, it is also fully functional.
In Scala variables are immutable by default.
Scala follows a Lazy Computation model where expressions are only evaluated when required. This increases performance by reducing compile time.

MongoDB: A collection in MongoDB is the same as a table in a relational databases.
A document in MongoDB is the same as a row in a relational databases.
A single entry in a collection is called a document.
A filter query fetches documents from a collection.
Operators are used to perform different filters or operations on a collection or a document.
Aggregation pipelines are used to perform aggregations or join operations on multiple collections.
Projection is used to select specific fields from a collection, reduce array data, and select specific fields from embedded documents.
GridFS is used to store large files.
PostgreSQL: PostgreSQL is an advanced, enterprise-class open-source object-relational database supporting full ACID compliance.
Multi-Version Concurrency Control (MVCC) enables non-blocking reads and concurrent writes with snapshot isolation.
PostgreSQL offers first-class support for semi-structured JSONB documents with GIN (Generalized Inverted Index) indexing.
Advanced capabilities include Common Table Expressions (WITH queries), Window Functions, and pgvector extension for AI embeddings.
Redis: Redis is an ultra-fast in-memory key-value data structure store used as a primary database, cache, message broker, and streaming engine.
Rich native data structures include Strings, Hashes, Lists, Sets, Sorted Sets (ZSETs), Bitmaps, and HyperLogLogs.
Persistence is provided via point-in-time RDB snapshots and append-only file (AOF) operation logging.
In-memory execution allows sub-millisecond read and write latency across millions of operations per second.
SQLite: SQLite is a serverless, self-contained, zero-configuration, transactional SQL database engine compiled directly into the application process.
Transactions are fully ACID-compliant even across operating system crashes or power interruptions.
Write-Ahead Logging (WAL) mode enables concurrent readers while a single writer is committing changes.
SQLite powers mobile applications on iOS and Android and client-side web databases via WebAssembly.
DuckDB: DuckDB is an in-process columnar SQL OLAP database management system built for high-performance analytical queries.
It features a vectorized query execution engine and processes queries directly on Apache Parquet, Arrow, and CSV files without data duplication.
Like SQLite for OLTP, DuckDB is serverless and embeds with zero external dependencies.
ClickHouse: ClickHouse is a column-oriented distributed database designed for real-time analytical reporting at petabyte scale.
Data in ClickHouse is physically stored sorted by primary key in MergeTree family engines with LZ4 and ZSTD compression.
Vectorized query execution processes billions of rows per second per server node.
Neo4j: Neo4j is a native graph database implementing the Property Graph Model with nodes, directional edges/relationships, and key-value properties.
It uses the Cypher declarative graph query language to traverse complex relationships with index-free adjacency in constant O(1) time per hop.
Graph databases are optimal for social networks, fraud detection, recommendation engines, and knowledge graphs.
DynamoDB: Amazon DynamoDB is a fully managed, serverless, key-value NoSQL database engineered for single-digit millisecond latency at any scale.
Tables are partitioned across storage nodes using a Partition Key (hash key) and an optional Sort Key (range key).
Global Secondary Indexes (GSIs) and Local Secondary Indexes (LSIs) provide flexible query projections.
Vector Databases: Vector databases (Pinecone, Qdrant, Milvus, Chroma) index high-dimensional mathematical embeddings generated by machine learning models.
Semantic similarity between concepts is calculated using distance metrics: Cosine Similarity, Euclidean Distance (L2), and Dot Product.
Approximate Nearest Neighbor (ANN) indexing structures such as HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) and IVFFlat provide sub-linear search speed.
